terms.grammar: verb, first conjugation: aliquid alicui probāre, or with an accusative and infinitive
evidence: Caes. BG 1.3.5: perfacile factū esse illīs probat
terms.comment: Properly “make good, make acceptable”: what is proved to someone is made credible to him, and the same verb is “approve” (Lewis & Short). “This proves that …” is documentō est (Traupman 366; see evidence).

evidence: Cic. Fam. 3.4.1: dēmōnstrāvit mē ā tē plūrimī fierī
terms.comment: Literally “point out”: to show by argument or description (Lewis & Short).

terms.gloss: prove (someone) wrong or guilty; prove (a thing) beyond question
evidence: Cic. Phil. 2.8: quō mē teste convincās?
terms.comment: Of persons, to convict of a fault or an error, the charge in the genitive; of things, to show a thing false or wrong beyond doubt (Lewis & Short).

phrases.latin: Perfacile factū esse illīs probat cōnāta perficere
phrases.english: He proves to them that it would be very easy to carry out their plans

phrases.latin: quod etsī difficile est probātū propter tam varia et tam multa tormenta fortūnae
phrases.english: and though this is hard to prove, because of fortune’s many and various torments

phrases.latin: sed quid oppōnās tandem, sī negem mē umquam ad tē istās litterās mīsisse? quō mē teste convincās?
phrases.english: But what will you set against it, if I deny ever having sent you that letter? With what witness will you prove me wrong?

sources: Lewis & Short: probo · Lewis & Short: demonstro · Lewis & Short: convinco
